questions.scenario: Contoso has an Azure container registry named acrcontoso in the East US region. The registry uses the Standard service tier. Developers in West Europe report slow image pulls.
questions.question: You need to provide a copy of the registry in West Europe while keeping a single registry name. What should you do first?

options.text: Change the registry service tier to Premium
options.why: Correct. Geo-replication is available only in the Premium tier, and the tier can be changed in place.

options.text: Create a second Standard registry in West Europe and import the images
options.why: This creates a separate registry with a different login server, so the single registry name is not kept.

options.text: Enable the admin user on the registry
options.why: The admin user controls authentication. It does not add a regional copy.

options.text: Create a private endpoint in West Europe
options.why: Private endpoints also require Premium and provide private access, not a regional replica.

questions.explanation: Upgrade the registry to Premium, then add a replication in West Europe. Pulls are served from the nearest replica.

questions.question: An Azure container app must pull images from an Azure container registry without storing a password. Which configuration should you use?

options.text: Assign the AcrPull role on the registry to the managed identity of the container app
options.why: Correct. A managed identity with AcrPull authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID and needs no stored password.

options.text: Enable the admin user and store its password as a secret
options.why: This stores a shared password, which the requirement prohibits.

options.text: Assign the Owner role on the resource group to all developers
options.why: This grants excessive permissions to people and does not configure the app's access.

options.text: Change the registry tier to Basic
options.why: The tier does not affect how the app authenticates.

questions.explanation: Use Microsoft Entra identities with the AcrPull role. Keep the registry admin user disabled.

questions.scenario: A container in Azure Container Instances processes invoices once each night. It must stop after it completes successfully and must start again only if it exits with an error.
questions.question: Which restart policy should you configure?

options.text: OnFailure
options.why: Correct. OnFailure restarts the container only when it exits with a non-zero exit code.

options.text: Always
options.why: Always restarts the container after every exit, so the job would run repeatedly and continue to incur charges.

options.text: Never
options.why: Never does not restart the container after a failure.

options.text: Unless-stopped
options.why: This is not a restart policy supported by Azure Container Instances.

questions.explanation: Container Instances supports Always (default), OnFailure and Never.

questions.question: A Linux container group in Azure Container Instances was created with 1 vCPU and 1.5 GB of memory. The workload now requires 4 GB of memory. What should you do?

options.text: Delete the container group and redeploy it with 4 GB of memory
options.why: Correct. CPU and memory are fixed properties of a container group, so a change requires a redeployment.

options.text: Configure an autoscale rule for the container group
options.why: Container Instances does not support autoscale rules.

options.text: Run az container update with the --memory parameter
options.why: There is no in-place update of memory for an existing container group.

options.text: Change the restart policy to Always
options.why: The restart policy does not change the allocated memory.

questions.explanation: Properties such as CPU, memory, OS type and restart policy require deleting and recreating the container group.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure Container Instances are true? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Containers in a container group share a lifecycle, network and storage volumes
options.why: Correct. A container group is scheduled on one host and shares these resources.

options.text: Charges are based on the vCPU and memory allocated, per second, while the group runs
options.why: Correct. Container Instances bills per second for allocated resources.

options.text: Container groups automatically add instances when CPU usage is high
options.why: Container Instances has no built-in autoscaling.

options.text: Container groups support deployment slots
options.why: Deployment slots are an App Service feature.

questions.explanation: For automatic scaling of containers, use Azure Container Apps or AKS.
